title: Real-time ingestion and streaming platforms
summary: How Kafka and its peers store event streams durably, how schemas and connectors keep them usable, and how streams land in warehouses and lakes.

blocks.text: A streaming platform is a durable, replayable, partitioned log. Producers append events; many independent consumers read at their own pace. That decoupling is the point: the CDC connector from chapter 17, a fraud service and a lakehouse sink can all read the same `orders` stream without knowing about each other.
18.1 Kafka's core model

items: **Partition**: an ordered, append-only log; a topic has many. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition.
**Key**: the producer hashes the key to choose a partition, so all events for one key stay ordered.
**Offset**: an event's position in its partition. Consumers track offsets, not the broker.
**Consumer group**: consumers sharing a group id split partitions among themselves; each partition is read by one member. Parallelism is capped by the partition count.
**Retention**: events are kept by time (`retention.ms`, default seven days) or size, whether read or not.

blocks.title: One topic, three partitions, two consumer groups
blocks.text:
p0: [0][1][2][3][4][5]   group 'lake-sink': c1(p0,p1) c2(p2)
 producers   p1: [0][1][2][3]
 (key hash)  p2: [0][1][2][3][4]      group 'fraud': f1(p0) f2(p1) f3(p2)

 each group commits its own offsets per partition;
 a 4th 'fraud' consumer would sit idle

Partition count is a long-term decision: more partitions mean more parallelism but more files, more leader elections and longer rebalances. Increasing partitions later changes the key-to-partition mapping, which breaks per-key ordering for keys that move.
18.2 Durability: replication and acks

Each partition has a **leader** and follower replicas on other brokers; a replication factor of 3 is the common production choice. Followers that keep up form the **in-sync replica set** (ISR). The producer setting `acks` decides when a write counts as successful.

head: Setting
Meaning
Trade-off
rows: Do not wait for the broker
Loss if leader dies before followers copy
Durable when combined with `min.insync.replicas=2` and RF 3

blocks.text: The **idempotent producer** (enabled by default in recent clients) attaches sequence numbers so broker-side retries do not create duplicates. **Transactions** let a producer write to several partitions and commit consumer offsets atomically; consumers with `isolation.level=read_committed` see only committed data (chapter 20 uses this for exactly-once). Modern Kafka manages metadata with its built-in **KRaft** quorum instead of ZooKeeper.
Log compaction

With `cleanup.policy=compact`, Kafka eventually keeps only the latest record per key and removes keys whose last record is a tombstone (null value). A compacted topic behaves like a changelog of current state: CDC topics, Kafka Streams state, reference data. Compaction runs in the background, so readers may still see older versions.
18.3 Kinesis, Pub/Sub and Redpanda

head: Platform
Unit of scale
Notes
rows: Per-shard read and write throughput limits; ordering per partition key within a shard; configurable retention
Topics and subscriptions, push or pull, ack deadlines, ordering keys; at-least-once by default, optional exactly-once delivery
Kafka-protocol compatible, C++, Raft per partition, no JVM; existing clients work
Managed Kafka (MSK, Confluent Cloud, Event Hubs Kafka API)

blocks.text: Check each service's current documentation for throughput quotas, message size limits and retention ranges; they differ and change. The design questions stay the same: what is the ordering scope, how is load spread, how long can I replay, and what does delivery guarantee.
Pub/Sub has no consumer-visible offsets; replay works by seeking a subscription to a timestamp or snapshot. Pipelines that assume Kafka-style offset checkpoints need a different recovery design.
18.4 Schema registry and compatibility

Bytes in a topic are meaningless without a schema. A **schema registry** (Confluent Schema Registry, Apicurio, AWS Glue Schema Registry) stores versioned Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema definitions per subject. In the Confluent wire format a message starts with a magic byte and a four-byte schema id, so consumers fetch the exact writer schema. The registry rejects new versions that violate the subject's compatibility mode.

head: Mode
Guarantee
Safe change example
Upgrade first
rows: New schema reads data written with the previous one
Add field with default, delete field
Previous schema reads data written with the new one
Add field, delete field that had a default
Add or remove fields that have defaults
Same, checked against all earlier versions

blocks.text: Renaming a field is a delete plus an add; under most modes it breaks someone. Topics retained for weeks may be replayed by consumers on the newest schema, which is why transitive modes matter for long retention.
18.5 Kafka Connect

Kafka Connect runs **source connectors** (Debezium, JDBC, S3) and **sink connectors** (Snowflake, Iceberg, S3, Elasticsearch) as configuration rather than code. A cluster of **workers** in distributed mode splits each connector into **tasks** and stores configs, offsets and status in internal topics, so tasks fail over between workers. **Converters** handle serialisation with the registry; **single message transforms** (SMTs) do light per-record changes such as routing or unwrapping the Debezium envelope.

blocks.title: Sink connector error handling (excerpt)

blocks.text: A dead-letter queue keeps poison messages from stopping a sink, but someone must own and drain it, or the DLQ becomes silent data loss.
18.6 Landing streams in warehouses and lakes

items: **Snowpipe Streaming** writes rows into Snowflake tables through channels, without staging files; each channel tracks an offset token so the client knows what is committed and can resume. The Snowflake Kafka connector can use it. Check the current documentation for its architecture and pricing.

**Iceberg sinks** (the Apache Iceberg Kafka Connect sink, Flink and Spark writers) buffer records into Parquet files and commit a snapshot periodically. Commit interval sets freshness, file count and metadata growth (chapters 19 and 25).
**Topic-to-table features** on some platforms materialise topics directly as Iceberg tables. The mechanism is the same buffered commit; check vendor documentation for guarantees.
**Bronze shape**: land the payload plus key, partition, offset and timestamp. Offsets give an exact replay point and a deduplication key.

blocks.title: Use case: clickstream to lakehouse and warehouse
blocks.text: A media site produces page views into a 24-partition topic keyed by session id, with Avro schemas under BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE. An Iceberg sink commits every few minutes into a bronze table; a Snowflake connector using Snowpipe Streaming feeds a small real-time dashboard table.
items: Both sinks are independent consumer groups; one being slow does not affect the other.
Seven days of retention allows replay after a sink bug.
Session-keyed partitioning keeps each session ordered for sessionisation (chapter 20).

blocks.title: Size and configure an events platform
blocks.text: An IoT company expects tens of thousands of device readings per second, must never lose acknowledged readings, needs per-device ordering, wants to replay two weeks of data, and lands into Iceberg. Choose topic layout and key, partition count reasoning, replication and acks, retention, schema compatibility mode, and how the Iceberg sink commits. Explain what you would monitor.
hints: What happens to ordering if you add partitions next year?
Which lag metric tells you the sink is falling behind?

items: Kafka is a partitioned, replicated log; ordering is per partition, and keys pick partitions.
Consumer groups split partitions; partition count caps parallelism.
`acks=all` with `min.insync.replicas` and RF 3 gives durability; idempotent producers stop retry duplicates.
Compaction keeps the latest value per key and turns topics into changelogs.
Schema registries enforce compatibility modes that decide upgrade order.
Sinks buffer and commit; commit frequency trades freshness for small files and cost.

blocks.q: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 10 consumers. What happens?
options: Each partition is shared by two consumers
Six consumers get one partition each and four sit idle
blocks.explain: Within a group each partition goes to one consumer, so parallelism is capped by partitions. Kafka never adds partitions automatically.

blocks.q: Which producer setup avoids losing acknowledged writes when a leader broker fails?
blocks.explain: `acks=all` waits for the in-sync replicas, and the minimum ISR setting ensures at least two copies exist. `acks=1` acknowledges before followers copy; compaction is about retention, not durability.

blocks.q: Under BACKWARD compatibility, which change is allowed and who upgrades first?
options: Changing a string to an int; consumers first
Adding a field with a default; consumers upgrade first
Adding a required field without default; producers first
blocks.explain: BACKWARD means readers on the new schema can read old data, which works when new fields have defaults; so consumers move first. A required field without default cannot be filled from old records.

blocks.q: What does a compacted Kafka topic guarantee?
options: At least the latest record per key is retained, and tombstoned keys are eventually removed
Only one record per key is ever visible
Messages are deleted after seven days
blocks.explain: Compaction is asynchronous, so older versions may still be read for a while; what is guaranteed is that the latest value per key survives. Time-based deletion is the `delete` policy.
